\chapter{Reaching Somebody}
\label{ch:ml-message}
\hlchaptermodality{110}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the telephone, a letter, the post, e-mail and the internet, and say an address aloud as far as the stop.}

From cold: five ways of reaching somebody, and the new letter that opens the first.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pha]{\ml{ഫ} — one character, met with the word that needs it}

\label{lesson:ML-S148-letter-pha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\ml{പ}} — say its sound.

One character this time. One only. It arrives with the word on the next page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഫ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഫ}} — \emph{pha}.

It is the breathed partner of \textbf{\ml{പ}}. Begin with the same lip closure, then let a puff of air follow the release: \textbf{\ml{പ}} \emph{pa}, \textbf{\ml{ഫ}} \emph{pha}.

Malayalam pairs stops this way — a plain one and a breathed one beside it. This one has not appeared in a headword yet; it arrives for the borrowed word on the next page.

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ഫ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{ഫ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which one carries the breath
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{പ}  ·  \ml{ഫ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{ഫ} three times, saying \emph{pha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pa}, then \emph{pha} — the same lips, one with a puff of air
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{ഫ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{pha}}.) Which letter is it the breathed partner of? (\textbf{\ml{പ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[phōṇ]{\ml{ഫോൺ} (phōṇ) — a telephone}

\label{lesson:ML-C110-phon}



\begin{quote}
Think of the thing you would pick up to reach somebody far away.

You are about to find you can nearly say it already.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}} (\emph{phōṇ}) — \textbf{a telephone}.

\textbf{Say it out loud and you will hear English.} It is \emph{phone}, borrowed whole, with the ending settled into Malayalam sounds: the \emph{n} at the close is made with the tongue curled back, not at the teeth.

\subsection*{Script Lens: three pieces}
Read it from left to right:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഫ}} & \emph{pha}, the breathed partner of \textbf{\ml{പ}} \\
\textbf{\ml{ോ}} & \emph{ō} \\
\textbf{\ml{ൺ}} & final retroflex \emph{ṇ}, with no following vowel \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first letter arrived on the page before this one. The last is the chillu you met inside \textbf{\ml{അരുൺ}} near the beginning of the book. Together they let the borrowed English word settle into Malayalam spelling: \textbf{\ml{ഫ} + \ml{ോ} + \ml{ൺ} = \ml{ഫോൺ}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}, with the tongue curled back at the end
  \item \emph{Say it:} which language the word came from
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ml{ഫ}}, \textbf{\ml{ോ}}, \textbf{\ml{ൺ}}, then the whole word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A telephone? (\textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}, \emph{phōṇ}.) Where does the word come from? (\textbf{English}.) Which character closes it? (\textbf{\ml{ൺ}}, final retroflex \emph{ṇ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kattŭ]{\ml{കത്ത്} — a letter}

\label{lesson:ML-C110-kattu}



\begin{quote}
Read and say the word for a telephone: \textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}.

Now think of the older way of reaching somebody who is far off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}} (\emph{kattŭ}) — \textbf{a letter}, the kind you write and send.

\textbf{Every piece of this word is one you can already read.} The doubled \textbf{\ml{ത്ത}} in the middle is the cluster you took apart in the school words, and the half-\emph{u} at the end is the one you close dozens of words with.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a shape that hides inside a word you know}]
\textbf{You have read these characters before, sitting inside another word.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}} & \emph{inside} \\
\textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}} & \emph{a letter} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Cover the first character of \textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}} and what is left looks exactly like \textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}}. The two words are not related, and the resemblance is worth meeting once so it cannot mislead you later.

\textbf{You were told how to read that pair when you learned it}: \emph{read the ends and not the fronts} — \textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}} and \textbf{\ml{പുറത്ത്}} end alike and differ at the front, which is where their meaning sits. \textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}} is a whole word rather than one of that pair, so the advice that sorts \emph{inside} from \emph{outside} is the same advice that keeps this one separate from both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kattŭ}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}} and \textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}}, and say which one means \emph{inside}
  \item \emph{Say it:} a letter, and a telephone, one after the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A letter? (\textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}}.) Does it have anything to do with \textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}}? (\textbf{No} — the shapes overlap and the words do not.) A telephone? (\textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tapāl]{\ml{തപാൽ} — the post}

\label{lesson:ML-C110-thapaal}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for a letter.

Then ask yourself what carries it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} (\emph{tapāl}) — \textbf{the post}: the service, and the word printed on the box you drop a letter into.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}} & the thing you write \\
\textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} & the thing that carries it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The ending is one you can already read.} \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} is the chillu you have met closing other words — a bare \emph{l} with no vowel after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tapāl}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the letter and the post, in that order
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} and name the character that closes it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The post? (\textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}}.) The thing you put in it? (\textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}}.) What closes \textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}}? (\textbf{The chillu \ml{ൽ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[imeyil — inṟarneṟṟŭ]{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ} — \ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}}

\label{lesson:ML-C110-imeyil}



\begin{quote}
Say the post, and the thing it carries.

Then say the mark that ends a written sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ}} (\emph{imeyil}) — \textbf{e-mail}.

\textbf{\ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}} (\emph{inṟarneṟṟŭ}) — \textbf{the internet}.

Both are English, borrowed whole and spelled in Malayalam letters, and both end the way you would expect: \textbf{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ}} on the chillu \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} you closed \textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} with, \textbf{\ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}} on the half-\emph{u}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} & carries \textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}} \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}} & carries \textbf{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you can already say an address out loud}]
An examiner may ask you to say an e-mail address, and the pieces are in hand: the letters, and the \textbf{full stop} you were taught with the other marks. A Malayalam speaker reading an address aloud names that mark exactly where it sits.

\textbf{The mark before the domain is a different matter.} This book has not given you a Malayalam name for it, for the same reason it gave you no Malayalam names for the punctuation marks: those names exist and are not written down here until they can be given with a source. What you can do already is spell the letters and place the stop.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{imeyil}, then \emph{inṟarneṟṟŭ}
  \item which of the two carries the other
  \item the mark you name aloud when reading an address
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
E-mail? (\textbf{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ}}.) The internet? (\textbf{\ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}}.) Which older pair do those two mirror? (\textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} carrying \textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sandesham enna oormma]{(phone, letter, post, e-mail, internet) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R110-message-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{telephone}, \emph{letter} and \emph{the post}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two ways of reaching somebody, a century apart}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}} carried by \textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}} & the older pair \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ}} carried by \textbf{\ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}} & the newer one \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The newer pair is borrowed and the older one is not}, which is the ordinary way a language takes in a new thing: the object arrives with its name attached. What is worth noticing is that the \emph{shape} of the pair did not change — a thing written, and a service that carries it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{All five are words you can now read.} The telephone added \textbf{\ml{ഫ}}, the breathed partner of \textbf{\ml{പ}}, and reused the final \textbf{\ml{ൺ}} from the opening chapters. The other four were already inside your script range.

You can now name the telephone, write and send a letter, and say an address aloud as far as the stop.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five words, in the order you met them
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}, and name its first and last consonants
  \item \emph{Say it:} which pair is borrowed and which is not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Telephone, letter, post? (\textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}, \textbf{\ml{കത്ത്}}, \textbf{\ml{തപാൽ}}.) E-mail and the internet? (\textbf{\ml{ഇമെയിൽ}, \ml{ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്}}.) Which new letter opens \textbf{\ml{ഫോൺ}}? (\textbf{\ml{ഫ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
